title: QUIC Internals
summary: QUIC is a UDP-based multiplexed transport with TLS 1.3 integrated into the handshake. It removes head-of-line blocking at the stream layer, enables 0-RTT, and is the substrate for HTTP/3 — but it changes how middleboxes, load balancers, and debugging work.

sections.title: Why QUIC exists
paragraphs: TCP + TLS + HTTP/2 still suffers connection setup cost (multiple RTTs) and head-of-line blocking: a lost TCP packet stalls all multiplexed HTTP/2 streams because TCP delivers a single ordered byte stream. On lossy mobile networks this dominates tail latency.

QUIC moves stream multiplexing into userspace over UDP. Each stream has independent flow control. A lost packet only blocks streams that need that data. Connection migration lets a client keep a connection ID when the IP/port changes (Wi-Fi to cellular).
TLS 1.3 is baked into the QUIC handshake, reducing round trips. 0-RTT can send application data on the first flight using prior session keys — with replay risks you must design for.
bullets: Stream-level multiplexing without TCP HOL blocking
Connection IDs enable migration across network paths

sections.title: Packets, frames, and streams
paragraphs: QUIC packets contain frames: STREAM, ACK, MAX_DATA, CONNECTION_CLOSE, CRYPTO, and others. Stream frames carry application bytes with offsets. Flow control exists at connection and stream scope.

Unlike TCP, much of the header is encrypted after the handshake, which breaks traditional middlebox parsing. Operators rely on Connection IDs, spin bit (limited), and endpoint telemetry rather than deep packet inspection of sequence numbers.

Loss detection uses ACK frames and probe timeouts rather than classic TCP dup-ACK alone. Implementations (Chromium, quiche, mvfst, quic-go) differ in pacing and congestion controllers (often CUBIC or BBR variants).

sections.title: HTTP/3 and deployment realities
paragraphs: HTTP/3 maps requests onto QUIC streams. Alt-Svc / HTTPS DNS records advertise h3. Clients often race TCP and QUIC and prefer the winner — so your edge must handle both.

Load balancing QUIC is harder: Connection IDs must be routed consistently, and retries after CID changes need shared state or CID-aware L4 balancers. UDP payload sizes and ICMP fragmentation interact poorly with poorly configured paths.
Debugging shifts from tcpdump-friendly cleartext headers to qlog and endpoint metrics. Plan observability before a wholesale h3 cutover.

sections.title: When QUIC helps — and when it does not
paragraphs: QUIC shines for browsers, APIs over lossy links, and connection migration. It helps less when you already terminate TLS at a nearby edge over excellent networks, or when enterprise firewalls block UDP 443.
gRPC and many internal RPC stacks still sit on HTTP/2 over TCP. Do not assume QUIC is universally available inside data centers — measure, then choose.

deepDive.title: 0-RTT replay and application safety
paragraphs: 0-RTT data can be replayed by an attacker who captured the first flight. Safe usage restricts 0-RTT to idempotent reads or servers that implement replay detection windows.
Design APIs so non-idempotent POSTs require 1-RTT keys. Document this in your client SDK — libraries will eagerly enable early data if you let them.

deepDive.title: Congestion control and pacing
paragraphs: Userspace congestion control must coexist with fair sharing on the bottleneck. BBR-style controllers estimate bandwidth and RTT; mis-tuned pacing can burst and induce loss.
Compare goodput and p99 under induced 1–2% loss against TCP+H2 before declaring victory.

expert.title: QUIC Internals — Expert notes
paragraphs: At the expert level, QUIC Internals intersects multi-region consistency, cost envelopes, and organizational constraints (team ownership, on-call load).
Write down the non-goals. Many outages come from optimizing a metric that was never the product requirement.

concepts: Stream multiplexing without TCP HOL blocking
HTTP/3 as application mapping on QUIC
practices: Support h2 and h3 at the edge during migration
Treat 0-RTT as opt-in for idempotent methods only
Use CID-aware load balancing for UDP/443
Collect qlog/metrics from both client and edge

examples.title: Chrome + Google edge
examples.description: Large-scale HTTP/3 deployment; connection migration across radio changes.

examples.title: Cloudflare / Fastly
examples.description: CDN edges terminating QUIC with careful CID routing and fallback to TCP.

keyTakeaways: QUIC fixes TCP HOL blocking for multiplexed apps by moving streams above UDP
Security handshake and transport are integrated — fewer RTTs, different ops model
Deployment success hinges on UDP path, LB, and observability readiness
whyItMatters: Modern public HTTP performance and mobile resilience increasingly depend on QUIC/HTTP/3. System designers who only reason about TCP will mis-predict latency and fail edge migrations.
reflectionQuestions: Which of your APIs are unsafe under 0-RTT replay?
How would you load-balance QUIC without sticky 4-tuples?
What metrics prove HTTP/3 improved p99 vs HTTP/2?
numbersToKnow: TCP+TLS 1.3: often 1–2 RTT before app data; QUIC can do 1-RTT (or 0-RTT)
Mobile networks: loss and path change make HOL blocking costly
UDP 443: commonly used; still blocked on some enterprise networks
